calculator.metaTitle: Fertilizer Dose Calculator — Urea, DAP & MOP per Acre/Kanal/Marla
calculator.metaDescription: Calculate exact urea, DAP and MOP doses per acre, kanal, marla or hectare — see how many 50 kg bags you need for wheat, rice, maize and more crops.

methodFaq.a: Phosphorus is immobile in soil, so the full P₂O₅ dose must come from DAP at sowing. DAP also contains 18% nitrogen, which counts toward the total nitrogen need — calculating DAP first lets us subtract that nitrogen before computing urea, so you never double-dose nitrogen.

methodFaq.q: How many bags of urea do I need per acre?
methodFaq.a: It depends on your crop's nitrogen requirement. For example, wheat needs 124 kg N per hectare (≈50 kg N per acre). Since urea contains 46% nitrogen, that's about 109 kg of urea per acre — roughly 2.2 bags of 50 kg each. Select your crop above and the calculator shows the exact bag count for your area.

methodFaq.q: How many bags of DAP do I need per acre?
methodFaq.a: DAP contains 18% nitrogen and 46% P₂O₅. For wheat (62 kg P₂O₅ per hectare ≈ 25 kg per acre), you need about 55 kg of DAP per acre — just over 1 bag of 50 kg. The calculator above computes the precise amount including the nitrogen bonus DAP provides.

methodFaq.q: How are kanal and marla converted?
methodFaq.a: 1 acre = 8 kanal = 160 marla, and 1 kanal = 20 marla. In metric: 1 acre = 0.4047 ha, 1 kanal = 0.0506 ha, 1 marla = 0.00253 ha. The calculator converts your area to hectares, applies the per-hectare dose, then scales back.

A crop is only selectable when its recommended NPK dose is verified against a published source. We would rather disable a crop than invent its figures — unverified crops are marked "data in review" until confirmed.

items.a: With the standard agronomic formula: fertilizer (kg) = (nutrient needed × 100) ÷ nutrient % in the fertilizer. We apply it DAP-first — phosphorus from DAP, then the remaining nitrogen from urea (accounting for DAP's 18% nitrogen), then potassium from MOP — and show every step.
items.q: How is the fertilizer dose calculated?

items.a: Acre, kanal, marla and hectare. Conversions used: 1 acre = 8 kanal = 160 marla, 1 kanal = 20 marla, 1 hectare = 2.471 acres.

Published provincial and research-institute recommendations (e.g. PAU package of practices), region-tagged. Every figure in the calculator carries its source citation, and crops without a verified source are marked 'data in review' rather than guessed.
items.q: Where do the crop nutrient figures come from?

items.a: No. It gives AI-assisted possibilities with uncertainty wording, but you should always confirm with your local agriculture officer before treating a crop — especially before spraying anything.
items.q: Is the Plant Doctor a replacement for an agronomist?

items.a: Yes — the calculator, libraries and guides are free. An account is only needed for features like saving diagnoses.
items.q: Is Fertilizer Dose free to use?
Can I mix urea and DAP together?
items.a: Yes, urea and DAP can be applied together as a basal dose at sowing. DAP provides phosphorus (46% P₂O₅) plus 18% nitrogen, while urea adds more nitrogen (46% N). A common practice is to mix them before broadcasting. However, avoid mixing urea with SSP (single super phosphate) in the same application if the mixture will sit — it can become lumpy. Always check your crop's recommended NPK ratio first.

items.q: What is basal dose in fertilizer?
items.a: The basal dose is the fertilizer applied at or before sowing/planting, worked into the soil. It typically includes the full phosphorus and potassium requirement plus a portion of nitrogen (usually 1/3 to 1/2). The remaining nitrogen is given as top-dressing later — for example, urea at tillering for wheat. Basal application ensures nutrients are available to young roots from day one.

items.q: DAP vs SSP — which is better?
items.a: It depends on your soil and crop. DAP (18-46-0) has higher phosphorus concentration (46% P₂O₅), so you need less product per acre — good for transport and handling. SSP (16% P₂O₅) also provides sulphur (~11%) and calcium (~19%), making it better for oilseeds, pulses, and sulphur-deficient soils. DAP is usually cheaper per kg of phosphorus, but SSP adds secondary nutrients. Use our Compare tool to check which is cheaper per kg of P₂O₅ at your local prices.

items.q: What is soil test based fertilizer dose?
items.a: A soil test measures your soil's existing nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, pH, and organic matter. Instead of using a blanket recommendation, the fertilizer dose is adjusted — if your soil already has high phosphorus, you apply less P fertilizer. This saves money and prevents over-fertilization. We recommend getting a soil test every 2-3 years through your local agriculture department. Our calculator uses standard recommendations; for soil-test-based precision doses, consult your local soil testing lab with these standard figures as a starting point.

method.title: The method, in plain words
method.desc: Build-up, maintenance, drawdown — the same logic soil labs use on health cards.

methodFaq.q: What is a soil test based fertilizer dose?
methodFaq.a: A blanket recommendation assumes an average soil. A soil test tells you what your field already holds: if phosphorus tests high, you can cut the P dose and save money; if it tests low, you raise it to build the soil up. This tool starts from a verified crop recommendation and applies exactly that logic — +30% for low-rated nutrients, base for medium, −25% for high.

methodFaq.q: Which soil-test values do I need?
methodFaq.a: Available phosphorus (Olsen method, mg/kg or ppm), available potassium (ammonium acetate method, kg/ha or ppm), organic carbon (%), and pH — the four values on a standard soil health card. You can enter P and K in either unit; the tool converts with the standard furrow-slice factor (×2.24).

methodFaq.q: Why is nitrogen rated from organic carbon?
methodFaq.a: Routine soil labs rarely report a mineral-nitrogen class, so extension systems use organic carbon as the proxy for native nitrogen-supplying capacity: more organic carbon means more nitrogen will mineralize during the season. It is a well-established proxy, but it is not a measured N value — the result is labeled as such.

methodFaq.q: Does an alkaline pH change my dose?
methodFaq.a: No — pH never changes the calculated dose here. Above pH 7.5, phosphorus increasingly precipitates as calcium and magnesium phosphates (P fixation), so placement matters: band the full phosphorus dose near the seed at sowing instead of broadcasting. The tool flags this as a note, not a dose change.

methodFaq.q: When should I not use the custom base dose?
methodFaq.a: The custom base option is generic guidance only — a starting point for crops with no verified recommendation in our database. If a verified crop×region dose exists, always use that instead; verified figures carry their published source.

method.title: Dosing by ppm, the way growers do it
method.desc: Commercial growers don't guess spoonfuls — they mix fertilizer to a target nutrient concentration in parts per million (ppm). This calculator brings the same method to home gardeners.

steps.d: Read the N-P-K numbers off the bag, e.g. 20-20-20, or enter a custom grade.
Houseplants and slow growers thrive on gentle rates (~100 ppm N); most container plants on regular rates (~150 ppm N); vigorous heavy feeders can take ~200 ppm N.
Dissolve the calculated grams in your watering can and water as usual, letting excess drain. Feed every watering at these rates, or half as often at double strength — never both.

sources.title: Where the feeding rates come from
items: UMass Extension — "Fertilizing Bedding Plant Seedlings" (D. Cox, 2011): bedding plants 200–250 ppm N constant feed; slow-growing types 100–150 ppm N until established.
Michigan State University Extension (E2186): container-grown plants — slow-release fertilizer plus supplemental liquid feed at 150–200 ppm N.
Virginia Tech SPES-744 — "The Basics of Fertilizer Calculations for Greenhouse Crops": the g/L = ppm ÷ (%N × 10) formula and worked 200 ppm N example.
sources.note: Presets use the low end of each published range, the conservative choice for home light levels. Always follow your product's label and your local extension service's advice.

faq.q: How much fertilizer do potted plants need?
faq.a: Most potted plants do well with a watering solution of 100–150 ppm nitrogen — roughly 0.5–1 g of 20-20-20 per litre of water. Heavy feeders like vigorous flowering annuals can take up to 200 ppm. Start gentle; you can always increase next time.

faq.q: Can I just use a spoon instead of weighing?
faq.a: A level teaspoon of granular fertilizer is roughly 5–6 g, but density varies by product, so spoons are only a rough guide. For small pots and seedlings, a cheap gram scale is far more reliable — a 50% spoon error is easy and enough to burn roots.

faq.q: Should I fertilize every time I water?
faq.a: At the gentle and regular rates above, yes — that is how commercial growers do it ("fertigate"). The alternative is feeding half as often at double strength. Don't do both: pick one schedule and watch the plants.

faq.q: What are the signs of too much fertilizer?
faq.a: Brown, crispy leaf edges, wilting despite wet soil, and a white crust on the medium surface. If you see these, flush the pot with plain water until it runs freely from the drainage holes, and skip the next feeding.

organic.intro: Organic fertilizers are plant and animal wastes that release nutrients as they decompose. They build soil, but they are dilute and inconsistent compared with mineral fertilizers. This page gives you typical nutrient ranges from published extension sources, and the limitations nobody should skip.
organic.whatBody1: Manures are plant and animal wastes used as sources of plant nutrients; they release those nutrients after decomposition (TNAU). The most widely used bulky organic manures are farmyard manure (FYM), compost and green manure. A second group — concentrated organic manures such as oilcakes, blood meal and bone meal — carries more nutrients per kilogram but is still far below mineral concentrations.
organic.whatBody2: The defining trait of organics is variability: the same material from two farms can differ several-fold in nutrient content depending on feedstock, preparation and storage. That is why this library shows ranges, never single label values, for organic materials.
organic.typesTitle: The four materials in this library
organic.typesIntro: Each card shows the typical N–P₂O₅–K₂O percentage range from published extension sources. Your batch will differ — these are starting points, not guarantees.
organic.compareTitle: How organics differ from mineral fertilizers
organic.compareIntro: Neither side is 'always better'. They do different jobs:

compareRows.mineral: High and exact — urea is 46% N, printed on the bag.
compareRows.organic: Low and variable — FYM is roughly 0.5–1.0% N, and every heap differs.

compareRows.mineral: Fast — nutrients are water-soluble and available within days.
compareRows.organic: Slow — microbes must mineralize them first; only ~30% of FYM nitrogen reaches the first crop (TNAU).

compareRows.mineral: Precise — the calculator can dose to the kilogram.
compareRows.organic: Approximate without a lab analysis of your specific batch.

compareRows.mineral: Little direct effect on soil structure or organic matter.
compareRows.organic: Improves structure, water-holding capacity and microbial activity.

compareRows.mineral: Concentrated — a few bags per acre.
compareRows.organic: Bulky — tonnes per hectare to move, spread and incorporate.

compareRows.mineral: Mostly taken up or lost within the season.
compareRows.organic: Long — feeds subsequent crops as decomposition continues.

uses: Building soil organic matter and structure over seasons — their strongest role.
Basal soil conditioning before sowing, especially on degraded or sandy soils.
Integrated nutrient management: organics for soil health plus mineral fertilizers for precise crop nutrition.
Nurseries, vegetables and high-value crops where soil biology pays back fastest.
Green manuring before transplanted rice, where dhaincha can add 130–185 kg N/ha of biologically fixed nitrogen.
organic.limitsTitle: Limitations — read before relying on them
limits: Low nutrient density: matching 100 kg N/ha with FYM needs 10–20 tonnes per hectare.
Variable composition: published ranges span 2–3× within a single material; only a lab analysis of your batch is precise.
Slow release: nutrients arrive over months, not days — they cannot rescue a mid-season deficiency.
Bulk and labour: tonnes to transport, spread and incorporate, versus bags of mineral fertilizer.
Quality risks: weed seeds and pathogens in poorly composted material; possible contaminants in municipal compost.
Not a drop-in replacement: 'manure instead of fertilizer' only works as a partial substitution inside a planned nutrient budget — never as an unqualified claim.
organic.warnBody: The calculator's organic section runs pure arithmetic on numbers YOU enter (your lab report or supplier label). It does not know your batch's real analysis, and it cannot account for slow release — treat its output as an upper bound on nutrients applied, not nutrients available to this season's crop. For precision dosing, get a lab analysis of your actual material.

guide.title: Measure land the honest way

formulas.name: Four sides + diagonal
formulas.formula: Split into two triangles along the diagonal; solve each with Heron's formula and add

guide.sqftTitle: How to calculate land area in square feet
guide.sqftBody: If your dimensions are in feet, multiply: area in square feet = length in feet × width in feet. Example: 100 ft × 50 ft = 5,000 sq ft. Divide by 43,560 for acres, or by 9 for square yards. For irregular plots, divide the land into rectangles and triangles, calculate each, and add them — or measure a diagonal and use the 4-side mode above.
guide.fourSideTitle: Why four sides alone are not enough
guide.fourSideBody: A quadrilateral can flex: the same four side lengths can enclose different areas depending on the angles. That is why no honest calculator gives an 'exact' area from sides alone. Measure one diagonal (corner to opposite corner) and the plot becomes two triangles — each with an exact area. Without a diagonal, only a labeled approximation is possible.
guide.irregularBody: Walk the field and divide it into simple shapes — rectangles, triangles, trapezoids. Measure each, calculate separately, and add the areas. The Irregular mode above does exactly this: add a section per part of your field and it totals them for you.
guide.conversionNote: Exact definitions. Regional units appear only where verified.
guide.sourcesBody: Universal units use exact SI and imperial definitions (1 acre = 4,046.8564224 m²; 1 hectare = 10,000 m²). Kanal and Marla use the Punjab revenue standard: 1 karam = 5.5 ft, 1 marla = 9 sq karam = 272.25 sq ft, 1 kanal = 20 marla = 5,445 sq ft. All calculations run in square meters internally and convert once to the display unit — no chained rounding.

faq.q: How do I calculate land area?
faq.a: Measure length and width in the same unit and multiply: area = length × width. For odd shapes, split the land into rectangles and triangles, calculate each, and add them up.

faq.q: How do I calculate agricultural land area?
faq.a: Use the same geometry, then convert to the unit your region uses — acres, hectares, or local units like kanal and marla in Pakistan. This calculator converts automatically and can send the result straight to the Fertilizer Dose Calculator.

faq.q: How do I calculate land area in square feet?
faq.a: Multiply length in feet by width in feet: 100 ft × 50 ft = 5,000 sq ft. One acre is 43,560 sq ft.

faq.q: Can four side lengths calculate an irregular plot exactly?
faq.a: No. Four sides alone cannot fix a quadrilateral's area — the shape can flex. Measure a diagonal as well and the plot splits into two exactly-solvable triangles. Without it, only a labeled approximation is possible.

faq.q: How do I convert acres to hectares?
faq.a: Multiply acres by 0.404686. One hectare equals 2.471 acres. Use the Converter mode above for any unit pair.

faq.q: What is the difference between an acre and a hectare?
faq.a: A hectare (10,000 m²) is about 2.47 times larger than an acre (4,047 m²). Hectares are standard in most countries; acres are common in Pakistan, India, Bangladesh and the US.

faq.q: Can I calculate irregular field area?
faq.a: Yes — use the Irregular mode: divide your field into rectangles, squares, triangles or trapezoids, enter each section, and the calculator totals them.

faq.q: Why do some traditional land units vary by region?
faq.a: Units like bigha, marla and kanal grew out of local revenue systems, so their size differs by province and convention. We only offer a regional unit where its conversion is verified — for example the Punjab revenue standard for kanal/marla — and we label the standard used.

faq.q: Can I use the calculated area in the Fertilizer Dose Calculator?
faq.a: Yes. Tap 'Use in Fertilizer Calculator' and your area, unit, country and region transfer automatically — no re-typing. You still pick your crop there, because area alone never determines fertilizer dose.

faq.q: Is this a legal land survey?
faq.a: No. This tool gives useful estimates from your own measurements for farming decisions. Legal boundaries, disputes and official records need a qualified surveyor or the land revenue authority.

mapArea.title: Map Area Calculator — Measure Land Area on the Map
mapArea.desc: Draw your field boundary on a free map and get its area instantly — in acres, hectares, square meters, and regional units. No account, no fees.
mapArea.metaTitle: Free Acreage Calculator Map — Measure Land Area on Map
mapArea.metaDescription: Free map area calculator: draw your field boundary on the map and measure land area in acres, hectares, m², Kanal and Marla. No sign-up needed.
mapArea.gateDescription: Choose your country so regional units (like Kanal and Marla in Pakistan) are shown, then open the interactive map. Tapping places boundary points — drag them to adjust.
mapArea.countryHint: Country only decides which regional units are shown. It never changes the map or your language.
mapArea.freeNote: Free forever — map data by OpenStreetMap contributors.
mapArea.mapAriaLabel: Interactive map for drawing a field boundary
mapArea.geoDenied: Location access was denied or unavailable — you can still navigate the map manually.
mapArea.tapHint: Tap a numbered point to remove it, or drag any point to move it.
mapArea.precisionNote: Useful estimate based on the points you placed — not survey-grade. Legal or official boundaries need a qualified local surveyor.
mapArea.useThisArea: Use This Area in Land Area Calculator
mapArea.privacyNote: Your boundary stays on this device. Only the area number is transferred — never your coordinates.
howSteps: Open the map and find your field — search is not needed; pan and zoom to it, or center on your location.
Tap the map to place boundary points around the field. Drag any point to adjust it; tap a numbered point to remove it.
With 3 or more points the area is calculated with geodesic (earth-curvature-correct) math — the same for any latitude.
Use the area in the Land Area Calculator, then in the Fertilizer Dose or Profit Calculator.
mapArea.mapNoteBody: The map uses OpenStreetMap, a free community-built world map — it is not Google Maps, and this tool has no affiliation with Google. Tiles load only while you measure.

faq.q: How does the map area calculator work?
faq.a: Tap the map to drop boundary points around your field. Once you have at least 3 points, the tool computes the enclosed area using geodesic mathematics that accounts for the earth's curvature — accurate at any latitude, unlike flat-screen measuring.

faq.q: Is the measured area survey-grade accurate?
faq.a: No. It is a useful estimate based on where you place the points and the map imagery alignment. For legal disputes, land records, or official transactions, hire a qualified local surveyor.

faq.q: Does this use Google Maps?
faq.a: No. The map is powered by OpenStreetMap, a free and open community map. There is no Google Maps integration and no affiliation with Google.

faq.q: Can I use the measured area for fertilizer calculation?
faq.a: Yes — the “Use This Area” button sends the measured area to the Land Area Calculator, from where it flows into the Fertilizer Dose Calculator and Profit Calculator. Area alone never produces a fertilizer recommendation; a verified crop and region are still required.

faq.q: Is my location or field boundary saved or shared?
faq.a: No. Boundary points live only in your browser's memory while you measure. Only the final area number is transferred between tools — your coordinates are never saved publicly, put in shareable links, or sent to our servers.

kitchenGarden.title: What to Grow This Month
kitchenGarden.metaTitle: Kitchen Garden Planner — What to Grow This Month
kitchenGarden.metaDescription: Plan a home kitchen garden: enter your plot size, pick your month, region and sunlight, and get vegetable and herb suggestions from verified planting windows — never guessed.
kitchenGarden.desc: Tell us your plot size, region and planting month. We suggest only vegetables and herbs with verified planting windows for that month — no invented varieties, no guessed calendars.
kitchenGarden.suggestionsCount: {n, plural, =0 {No options} one {# option} other {# options}} for {month} in {region}
kitchenGarden.selectHint: Tick the crops you want to grow to build your plan below.
kitchenGarden.emptyTitle: No verified planting data for this selection
kitchenGarden.emptyBody: We have no verified vegetable or herb planting windows for {region} in {month} yet. We never guess — try a different month or region, or browse the full planting calendar as more regional data gets verified.
kitchenGarden.sunlightGapNote: Sunlight needs are not recorded for these crops yet, so your sunlight preference could not be applied as a filter. All month-appropriate options are shown.
kitchenGarden.shareTotal: Shares add up to {total}% — they should total 100%.
kitchenGarden.bedAssumptionNote: Layout math only: with {bedWidth} m-wide beds and {pathWidth} m paths, about {pct}% of your plot is plantable bed area — roughly {bedMeters} m of bed length. Bed width and path width are your own adjustable assumptions, not crop guidance.
kitchenGarden.spacingNote: Row and plant spacing is not verified for these crops yet — check your local agricultural extension guidance before finalizing spacing.
kitchenGarden.savedPlotNote: {sqm} m² kitchen garden plan for {month}, {region}; {count} crop(s) selected.

faq.q: What can I plant in a small kitchen garden this month?
faq.a: It depends on your region and the month. Enter your plot details above and the planner lists only vegetables and herbs with verified planting windows for your selection — with the source named on every suggestion.

faq.q: Does the planner tell me how far apart to plant?
faq.a: Not yet. Row and plant spacing has not been verified for these crops in our data, so the planner says so honestly instead of inventing numbers. Check your local agricultural extension guidance for spacing.

faq.q: How is this different from the planting calendar?
faq.a: The planting calendar shows every verified window for a region and month, including field crops. This planner narrows it to vegetables and herbs suitable for a home garden, adds your plot size and sunlight, and turns the picks into a simple layout plan you can save to My Garden.

faq.q: Can I use my land area measurement here?
faq.a: Yes. The Land Area Calculator's “Plan a Kitchen Garden” button sends your measured area straight into this planner.

faq.q: Where is my plan stored?
faq.a: In your browser's My Garden (local storage) when you press “Save plan to My Garden”, just like saved plots from the Land Area Calculator. Sign in to sync it across devices.

suggestions.rulesToggle: What we accept — and what we reject

suggestions.accept4: Your own field experience — written honestly (see below)
suggestions.reject1: Claims with no source at all

contributors.metaDescription: Meet the farmers and experts improving Fertilizer Dose: verified contributors, badges and the leaderboard.
contributors.subtitle: Farmers and experts who share verified knowledge with the community — rewarded with recognition, never money.
contributors.howItWorksBody: Share a translation fix or crop data with an official source. When our team approves it, your name and photo appear on the relevant pages, your approved count grows, and you earn badges: 🌱 Contributor (1), 🌾 Trusted Farmer (5, with priority review), 🏅 Agri Expert (20, with a printable certificate).
